newsitem.title: GERMANY: G7 aims to help small firms trade in cyberspace.
newsitem.headline: G7 aims to help small firms trade in cyberspace.

text.p: German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt on Monday unveiled an initiative to help small firms use the Internet as he opened an electronic commerce conference sponsored by the Group of Seven industrialised nations.

The three-day conference in Bonn is the first to be held as a result of a G7 project launched two years ago that aims to come up with international measures to promote the development of trade on the global Internet computer network.
"Everyone on the global network gains from achieving as large a number of participants as possible," Rexrodt said in a speech prepared for delivery at the conference opening in Bonn.
"All of the G7 ministers believe that it is of the utmost importance for our economies that particularly small and mid-sized companies find their way in the Information Society in time," he added.

The conference will host a series of workshops with politicians, industry experts, and small and medium-sized companies on issues ranging from data security and Internet regulation to questions of copyright and liability.

Rexrodt, outlining a German programme that will accompany a similar EU effort to be launched next week, said Bonn wanted to do more to help companies help themselves by offering training and consulting.
"Particularly small and mid-sized companies need extra stimulus for their entry onto the global marketplace," said Rexrodt. "Therefore I am planning a national initiative on electronic commerce."

Mario Monti, EU commissioner for the single market and taxation, said while 98 percent of large European corporations were hooked up to the Internet this was true for just four percent of small and mid-sized enterprises (SMEs).
At the same time, the global electronic marketplace was growing 60 percent a year and could reach a trade volume of some 1.5 trillion ecus ($1.7 trillion) by the turn of the century, he said.

This rapid expansion is demonstrated by the increase in the number of people with Internet access, which is estimated to rise to 250 million in the year 2000 from around 86 million at the end of last year.
"SMEs will only be able to realise their full potential in the cyber-economy if they are fully aware of the opportunities," Monti said.
"It is essential for policy-makers to ensure electronic commerce can develop under optimal conditions, so that its benefits are maximised, notably in terms of job creation and welfare enhancement."
Monti said there must be a secure European regulatory framework for electronic commerce based on the principles of the European single market.

Differing national regulations could inhibit firms seeking to engage in cross-border electronic trade, he said, adding that contract regulations in some EU countries were "not appropriate for an electronic commerce environment".
The main issues of concern to Europeans were questions of personal data security and the legal certainty and ability for redress in electronic trade.

Companies were increasingly concerned about on-line piracy and needed intellectual property protection. EU governments should also refrain from special taxes on electronic trade as standard value added tax rules already applied.
"There is no need to introduce new forms of tax, such as a 'bit tax', within the EU," he said.
The G7 comprises the United States, Japan, Germany, France, Italy, Britain and Canada. ($ = 0.865 European Currency Unit ECUs)
